\chapter{The Hand and the Foot}
\label{ch:sa-body-more}
\hlchaptermodality{25}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five more parts of the body in Sanskrit, and name the sound law that ties three of them to their English cousins.}

Complete SA-C25-hair and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hastaḥ]{\sk{हस्तः} (hastaḥ) — hand}

\label{lesson:SA-C25-hand}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{dīpaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{हस्तः}}
\textbf{\sk{हस्तः}} (\emph{hastaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}hand\textquotedblright{}.

You have \sk{अक्षि}, \sk{कर्णः}, \sk{मुखम्}, \sk{नासिका} and \sk{हृदयम्}. \textbf{\sk{हस्तः}} adds the hand.

Its cousins run west rather than into Europe: Avestan \emph{zasta}, Old Persian \emph{dasta}, and modern Persian \emph{dast}, all \textquotedblleft{}hand\textquotedblright{}. Latin went its own way with \emph{manus} and shares nothing with this word at all — a reminder that the family tree branches, and that two languages can both be cousins of Sanskrit without being cousins of each other in any given word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A sixth part of the body, and a cousin found next door rather than in Rome.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hastaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{hastaḥ}, then \emph{akṣi} and \emph{hastaḥ} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{हस्तः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}hand\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pādaḥ]{\sk{पादः} (pādaḥ) — foot}

\label{lesson:SA-C25-foot}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{hastaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पादः}}
\textbf{\sk{पादः}} (\emph{pādaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}foot\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{पादः}} is one of the most travelled words in this book. Latin \emph{pēs}, in its other forms \emph{pedem} — whence \emph{pedal}, \emph{pedestrian}, \emph{biped}. Greek \emph{pous}, \emph{podos} — whence \emph{podium}, \emph{tripod}, \emph{octopus}, the eight-foot.

And English \emph{foot}, which looks unlike the rest until you apply the same sound law you met at \sk{पिता} and \emph{father}: an old \emph{p} becomes \emph{f} in the Germanic branch. \emph{Pādaḥ} and \emph{foot} are the same word, worn differently. Masculine \textbf{-\sk{अः}}, like \sk{हस्तः}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word whose cousins you can now predict rather than be told.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pādaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pādaḥ}, then \emph{pitā}, and name the sound law both share with their English cousins
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{पादः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}foot\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śiraḥ]{\sk{शिरः} (śiraḥ) — head}

\label{lesson:SA-C25-head}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{pādaḥ} mean, and what did \emph{hastaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{शिरः}}
\textbf{\sk{शिरः}} (\emph{śiraḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{शिरः}} is the head. The old family it belongs to gathered around a sense of \textquotedblleft{}head, horn\textquotedblright{}: Greek \emph{kara}, \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}, and Latin \emph{cerebrum}, \textquotedblleft{}brain\textquotedblright{}, sit in it, and so — further out — does English \emph{horn}.

Sanskrit has a second head-word, \emph{mūrdhan}, for the top or the summit of a thing. \sk{शिरः} is the ordinary one: the head you nod, the head you bow when you say \sk{नमस्ते}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of five, and the bow you already knew has a body part in it now.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śiraḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{śiraḥ}, then say \emph{namaste} and name what bends
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{शिरः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dantaḥ]{\sk{दन्तः} (dantaḥ) — tooth}

\label{lesson:SA-C25-tooth}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{śiraḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{दन्तः}}
\textbf{\sk{दन्तः}} (\emph{dantaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}tooth\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{दन्तः}} is a tooth, and its family is as secure as \sk{पादः}. Latin \emph{dens}, in its other forms \emph{dentem} — whence \emph{dentist}, \emph{dental}, \emph{trident}, the three-tooth. Greek \emph{odous}, \emph{odontos} — whence \emph{mastodon}.

English \emph{tooth} belongs here too, by the same Germanic shift that turned \emph{p} into \emph{f}: an old \emph{d} becomes \emph{t}. So \sk{दन्तः}, \emph{dens} and \emph{tooth} are three worn copies of one word, and you have now seen the same machinery produce \sk{पिता}/\emph{father}, \sk{पादः}/\emph{foot} and \sk{दन्तः}/\emph{tooth}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A third demonstration of one sound law, on a word you can point at.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dantaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dantaḥ}, then \emph{pādaḥ}, then \emph{pitā} — three words, one shift
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{दन्तः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}tooth\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[keśaḥ]{\sk{केशः} (keśaḥ) — hair (of the head)}

\label{lesson:SA-C25-hair}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of this run: what did \emph{dantaḥ} mean, and what did \emph{śiraḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{केशः}}
\textbf{\sk{केशः}} (\emph{keśaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}hair (of the head)\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{केशः}} is the hair on the head — the hair that grows out of \sk{शिरः}.

And here the trail stops. No secure cousin has been found for \sk{केशः} outside India: scholars have proposed several and settled on none. That is worth meeting on purpose, because the last four lessons made travel look easy. Some words have a history we can reconstruct in detail; some have one we cannot reconstruct at all. \sk{कर्णः}, the ear, was the same case. Masculine \textbf{-\sk{अः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five more parts of the body: hand, foot, head, tooth, hair.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, and name the one with no known cousins
\end{itemize}
